summary: This informational memo documents MAPOS 16, a multiple access protocol that carries datagrams in HDLC frames with 16-bit addressing over SONET/SDH.

eli5.summary: The same shared fiber rules, but with longer addresses so more devices fit.

questions: what is the mapos 16 frame format
how are ip multicast addresses mapped in mapos 16
subtitle: MAPOS with a 16-bit address field, so a shared SONET/SDH network can hold far more nodes.

tldr.problem: MAPOS version 1 keeps PPP-compatible frames and so has a narrow 8-bit address field, which limits how many nodes can share a SONET/SDH network.
tldr.mechanism: MAPOS 16 uses HDLC-like framing with a 16-bit address field, drops the control field to keep the header 32-bit aligned, and places 16-bit addresses in the low bits of the existing 32-bit address fields of the other MAPOS protocols.
tldr.outcome: The wider address space leaves the MAPOS protocol family (ARP, UNARP, NSP and SSP) essentially unchanged. The memo is informational and not an IETF product.

today: RFC 2175 is an Informational memo and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is not a standards-track document.

sections.title: MAPOS and the Move to 16 Bits
sections.content:
MAPOS is a multiple access protocol that carries HDLC frames over SONET/SDH. It gives multiple access to SONET/SDH, which is inherently point-to-point. MAPOS version 1 (RFC 2171) keeps its frame format compatible with conventional PPP, which results in a narrow 8-bit address field. MAPOS 16 widens the address space to 16 bits.

The authors state that the memo is not the product of an IETF working group and is not a standards-track document, so it has not necessarily had the in-depth community review that standards-track documents receive.
sections.eli5: MAPOS lets many computers share one fiber line instead of just two. The new version just gives each computer a longer address.

sections.title: The MAPOS 16 Frame
sections.content:
Framing follows the HDLC-like framing used in PPP over SONET/SDH (RFC 1662), with two changes: the address field is 16 bits, and the MAPOS version 1 control field is omitted to keep the header 32-bit aligned. LLC and SNAP are not used. Fields are sent left to right.

  • Flag: 01111110 (0x7E) begins and ends each frame. One flag may end one frame and start the next, and flags are sent continuously when the line is idle.
  • Address: the destination HDLC address, 16 bits, used by a switch to forward the frame.
  • Protocol: 16 bits, naming the protocol of the datagram in the information field. Values come from Assigned Numbers and MAPOS Version 1 Assigned Numbers.
  • Information: the datagram, which shall not exceed 65,280 (64K - 256) octets.
  • FCS: 16 bits by default, optionally 32 bits, calculated over the address, protocol and information fields before escape conversion.
sections.eli5: Each message is wrapped like a parcel: a start marker, an address, a note saying what is inside, the contents, a check number, and an end marker.

sections.title: The 16-Bit Address
sections.content:
The least significant bit of the first byte indicates continuation of the field and must always be 0. The least significant bit of the second byte marks the end of the field and must always be 1. These are the two EA bits. The most significant bit of the first byte tells unicast from multicast: 0 means unicast, 1 means multicast or broadcast. The remaining thirteen bits carry the destination node address (unicast) or the group address (multicast).

The address 0xFEFF means broadcast, and 0x0001 is reserved to identify the control processor inside a switch. Frames with an invalid address should be silently discarded.

For IP multicast, the thirteen address bits must hold the lowest-order thirteen bits of the IP multicast group address. If those thirteen bits are all zeros or all ones, the address 1111 1110 1111 1101 should be used instead.
sections.eli5: The address has a special first bit that says whether the message is for one house or for a whole group, and the rest of the bits are the house or group number.

sections.title: Octet Stuffing and Inter-frame Fill
sections.content:
MAPOS 16 uses the same octet stuffing as MAPOS version 1. Because SONET/SDH provides transparency, the Async-Control-Character-Map is not used. After the FCS is computed, any 0x7E other than the flags becomes 0x7D 0x5E, and any 0x7D becomes 0x7D 0x5D. The receiver reverses this before computing the FCS.

After the FCS a sender must continuously send the flag sequence as inter-frame fill, and receivers silently discard it. If a DMA under-run occurs, the sender must abort the frame and keep sending flags to signal the error.
sections.eli5: If the data happens to look like the start marker, it gets a small disguise so nobody mistakes it, and the receiver removes the disguise.

sections.title: Effect on the MAPOS Protocol Family
sections.content: ARP, UNARP, NSP and SSP already use 32-bit address fields for the 8-bit MAPOS address, so the wider address needs no change to them. Each protocol puts the 16-bit address in the least significant place of its 32-bit field. In MAPOS ARP and UNARP this applies to the sender and target HDLC addresses. In an NSP address assignment packet the rest of the field is padded with zeros. In an SSP route entry the 16-bit address sits in the least significant bytes.
sections.eli5: The old forms had room for long numbers already, so the new short-but-longer address just slides into the end of the box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says only that security issues are not discussed in it. Anyone deploying MAPOS 16 would need to look elsewhere for guidance, since this RFC gives none.
sections.eli5: The memo does not say anything about keeping the line safe from snoopers.
